title: How the Negro Leagues Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the history of the Negro Leagues, the all-Black professional baseball leagues that arose after baseball's unwritten color barrier took hold in 1890. They trace the post-Civil War context of Jim Crow segregation, early Black players in the white major leagues (Moses Fleetwood Walker and Weldy Walker with the Toledo Blue Stockings, and the 1887 Toledo-White Sox dispute involving Cap Anson), barnstorming, Rube Foster's founding of the first Negro National League in 1920, the numbers-racket owners behind the second Negro National League and the Golden Age, the Homestead Grays and Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, the East-West All-Star game, the decline after Foster's breakdown and the Depression, and the integration of the major leagues led by Branch Rickey and Jackie Robinson in 1947. The episode closes with listener mail about mnemonic devices and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the Negro Leagues
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of the Negro Leagues as a story about history and overcoming adversity, then give a brief primer on slavery, Reconstruction, and the rise of Jim Crow.

segments.title: Early Black players in white baseball
segments.summary: Discussion of the 1867 Philadelphia Black team rejected by the National Association of Baseball Players, and individual Black players including the Walker brothers with Toledo, and the 1887 Toledo-Chicago White Sox dispute involving Cap Anson.

segments.title: The 1890 unwritten color ban
segments.summary: Black players in the major and minor leagues such as Bud Fowler, Frank Grant, and George Stovey faced pressure and hate mail, and by 1890 Black players were effectively pushed out through an unwritten, non-official agreement.

segments.title: Barnstorming and the founding of the first Negro National League
segments.summary: Black teams barnstormed across the country to earn money. Rube Foster organized seven Black-owned teams in Kansas City in 1920 to form a league, and the league held a Negro League World Series.

segments.title: Collapse of the first league and Rube Foster's decline
segments.summary: Rube Foster suffered gas poisoning in Indianapolis, later became institutionalized, and died in 1930. Combined with the Depression, the first league unraveled. Attendance and finances were limited.

segments.title: Numbers racket owners and the Golden Age
segments.summary: Numbers game operators, including Gus Greenlee who bought the Pittsburgh Crawfords, financed a second Negro National League in 1933, starting the Golden Age. The Homestead Grays won nine straight pennants, and the East-West All-Star Game became the big event.

segments.title: Satchel Paige and the Negro leagues stars
segments.summary: Satchel Paige is described as a dominant pitcher with pinpoint control and an invented hesitation pitch, who pitched into his late forties and fifties and was paid well. Estimated career stats are discussed, along with his later signing by the Atlanta Braves.

segments.title: Branch Rickey, Jackie Robinson, and integration
segments.summary: Branch Rickey of the Brooklyn Dodgers chose Jackie Robinson to break the color barrier in 1947. Hosts discuss World War II service by Black soldiers, the rapid integration that followed, and the bittersweet end of the Negro Leagues.

segments.title: Nicknames and closing remarks on the Negro Leagues
segments.summary: Hosts list colorful Negro league player nicknames and point listeners to further resources on the topic, including MLB.com articles and negroleaguebaseball.com.

segments.title: Listener mail: mnemonic devices
segments.summary: Katie from West Texas corrects the word mnemonic and shares the mnemonic 'Kings play chess on fine green silk' for taxonomic ranks.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
